conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee, one of your hospital doctors. You’re here because of abdominal pain, nausea, and diarrhea. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. I’ve had this pain in my upper belly for a few days. It feels like my usual pancreatitis flare—radiates to my back, constant. I’ve also had fevers, nausea, and loose stools. I thought I had a stomach bug.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Your labs show your white count is up, and your lactate is elevated at 3.7, which suggests your body is under stress. Your lipase is normal, so it might not be pancreatitis this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But it feels just like my pancreatitis. I’ve had this before. Could it still be that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s possible, but we need to look deeper. A CT scan showed significant wall thickening in your colon—especially the sigmoid and descending parts. This could be colitis, either from infection or poor blood flow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Colitis? Like C. diff? I’ve had that before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We tested for C. diff—it came back negative. No other infections were found in your stool either. But your lactate went up to 5.1, and you’re tachycardic. We’re moving you to the ICU for closer monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: ICU? That sounds serious. Am I in danger?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re being cautious. Your body is stressed, and we need to make sure your organs are getting enough blood. We’re starting IV fluids and antibiotics—vancomycin, ceftazidime, and metronidazole—just in case it’s an infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your lactate is down to 3.2 today—that’s a good sign. But it went back up to 5.4 last night. We’re concerned about ischemic colitis—when part of the colon doesn’t get enough blood.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that from low blood pressure? I remember feeling dizzy when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We think a drop in blood pressure may have reduced blood flow to your colon. We did a CTA, and while your arteries are open, the colon wall is severely thickened and inflamed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not an infection? Why the antibiotics then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can’t rule out infection completely, and with your history, we’re being cautious. But right now, ischemic colitis is the leading concern.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re seeing dark stools, and your hemoglobin dropped by 3 points. You’ve lost some blood from the colon. We’re giving you two units of blood to stabilize you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t know I was bleeding. Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s serious, but we caught it early. Your levels are stable now. We’re also watching your clotting—your INR was high at 4.3, but it’s coming back down on its own.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had clotting issues before. Should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. It’s likely a reaction to the inflammation. We’re not giving blood products unless needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re having trouble keeping your IVs in. You’ve had a midline, but we can’t draw labs from it. We’re going to place a PICC line for better access.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had PICCs before. They’ve caused clots. Is it safe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We know your history. We’re using ultrasound and fluoroscopy. There’s some central vein narrowing, but we’ll navigate carefully.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The PICC is in—right brachial vein, tip in the superior vena cava. It’s working well for fluids and labs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. Can I finally eat something? I’m so tired of IV fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to start you on clear liquids. If you tolerate it, we’ll advance slowly. But your colon is still inflamed, so we need to be cautious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your CRP is very high—138—showing significant inflammation. But your lactate is now normal at 1.0. That’s a big improvement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m getting better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Your vital signs are stable, pain is improving, and labs are trending in the right direction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re scheduling an EGD and sigmoidoscopy tomorrow to look at your stomach and colon directly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that tell us what caused this?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It will help. We’ll take biopsies to rule out inflammatory conditions and check for gastritis, which you’ve had before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The EGD showed mild gastritis and a small erosion at the stomach entrance. The sigmoidoscopy showed ulceration and inflammation in the splenic flexure—consistent with colitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s confirmed? Is it ischemic or infectious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Biopsies are pending, but given your history, blood pressure drop, and clean infection workup, ischemic colitis is most likely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my liver tests? They were high.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your alkaline phosphatase and GGT are elevated. GI wants you to follow up with MRCP and liver enzyme tests after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re switching your IV antibiotics to oral cipro and metronidazole for one more week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my pain meds? I’m still uncomfortable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re transitioning you back to your home pain meds—tramadol. We’ll keep it scheduled for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your hemoglobin is stable at 9.8. You’re tolerating a soft diet, and your bowel movements are forming.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning for discharge in a couple of days. You’ll need a colonoscopy in a few weeks to fully evaluate the colon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re stopping IV fluids. You’re eating well and hydrated. We’ll remove the PICC tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. I don’t want another clot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll remove it safely. Given your history, we’re not leaving it in or placing a port for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your PICC is out. No issues. You’re walking well, pain is mild, and labs are good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my other meds? I take a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re back on all your home meds—Seroquel, amitriptyline, omeprazole, lisinopril, amlodipine, clonidine as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my Creon for digestion?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, back on Creon. And we’re continuing omeprazole for your gastritis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Discharge is tomorrow. You’ll follow up with your PCP, GI, and get a colonoscopy in a few weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What signs should I watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Fever, severe pain, or bloody stools—call your doctor. Otherwise, rest and take meds as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’m glad this is over.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad too. You did well. Your wife will be here tomorrow to take you home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared to go home. Here’s your discharge summary and prescriptions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll follow up with all my doctors. I don’t want to come back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll make sure your PCP has your care plan. If you have another pain flare, go to the ER—mention your protocol.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we hope to see you only in clinic.
